title: Hybrid Residency: Authorization, Audit Correlation, and Evidence Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary:

This playbook describes Redwood Inference’s cross-cutting approach for handling authorization (RBAC/ABAC), correlated audit logging, evidence preparation for audits, and special considerations when audit data transits or resides across jurisdictional boundaries (hybrid residency). It also prescribes Secure SDLC checkpoints and incident-response evidence preservation steps for authorization-related changes. The target audience is security engineers, compliance owners, SREs, and platform/product teams.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Ensure that access-control decisions, the observable events that prove those decisions, and the packaged evidence needed for compliance reviews are consistently generated, retained, and correlated across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Scope: Applies to all Redwood services that authenticate or authorize human or machine actors, audit/log generation pipelines, evidence assembly activities for compliance/regulatory audits, and deployment models where log storage may cross regions or cloud boundaries (hosted, dedicated, private/VPC).

Principles (high level):
1. Single source of truth for entitlement: Primary user/group/role definitions live in the central identity directory (Identity Service) and are joined to local role mappings via well-defined sync processes.
2. Correlatable events: Every authorization decision must generate a minimally sufficient audit event that includes identity, role, decision reason, resource identifier, and request context (IP/region, model/route, request id).
3. Evidence first: Compliance packages are assembled from canonical events and artifacts; ad-hoc exports are discouraged.
4. Jurisdiction-aware retention: Retention, pseudonymization, and egress controls depend on data residency requirements and must be applied at the earliest possible ingestion point.
5. Change gating: Authorization policy changes that affect production must pass Secure SDLC gates (review, test, canary, and evidence capture).

Ownership and stakeholders:
- Evidence owner: Compliance (legal + security liaison) — responsible for audit packaging and sign-off.
- Operational owner: Platform SRE — responsible for log pipeline availability and retention enforcement.
- Policy owner: Identity & Access Management (IAM) team — owns role definitions and mappings.
- Review cadence: Quarterly tabletop reviews; ad-hoc after major auth/system changes.

Minimum required audit event schema (each audit entry must contain these fields):
- event_id (UUID)
- timestamp (ISO-8601)
- actor_id (internal user id or service principal)
- actor_type (human | service | admin-tool)
- authn_method (OIDC | SAML | APIKey | Cert)
- roles_evaluated (list)
- decision (allow | deny | step-up | unknown)
- resource (canonical resource path)
- action (API route / RPC method / console action)
- request_id (correlating trace id)
- client_ip and geo: (if available)
- region_tag: (hosting region or customer region)
- reason or policy_reference (short pointer to policy rule id)
- evidence_refs (list of artifact ids, see Evidence artifacts section)

Correlation matrix (how artifacts map to compliance needs):
- Authz decision event -> Proof of authorization: event_id, policy_reference, roles_evaluated, decision.
- Identity proof -> Identity repository snapshot: user record hash, last-authn timestamp, MFA status.
- Provisioning proof -> Provisioning audit log + change request id (CR-<number>).
- Config proof -> Configuration-as-code (Git commit + diff) and change approval notes.
- Telemetry proof -> Service request traces, request payload/redaction snapshot, and model invocation references.

Evidence artifacts (catalog):
- Canonical authz events (time-ordered) — primary artifact.
- Identity snapshots (PII minimized) — for auditors: account id, account age, current role set, MFA status.
- Git commits and PR approvals for policy or infra changes.
- Release and canary rollout logs showing affected host(s)/region(s).
- Log retention manifest: where the logs are stored, retention policy id, and checksum.
- Packaging manifest (see Packaging checklist).

Packaging checklist (minimum):
1. Date range and scope (UTC timestamps).
2. Canonical event export (newline-delimited JSON) with schema version.
3. Hash manifest (SHA-256 checksum for each artifact).
4. Mapping document linking event_ids to PRs/CRs (where applicable).
5. Pseudonymization summary if PII redacted (method and salt location).
6. Retention compliance statement (policy id and justification).
7. Evidence owner sign-off notes (name, email, date).

Data residency and hybrid residency controls:
- Ingest-time tagging: Every audit event must be tagged with region_tag and customer_region where applicable. Ingest agents apply tags before log export.
- Region-bound storage policy: For data classified as region-restricted, the pipeline must block export to non-authorized regions unless an exception exists.
- Pseudonymization at edge: For jurisdictions that forbid cross-border transfer of direct identifiers, pseudonymize (deterministic hashing with a rotating salt stored in the KMS) before forwarding.
- Cross-border evidence requests: To provide evidence for an auditor in another jurisdiction, follow the cross-border evidence exception flow (see Risk & Exceptions section below).

Retention matrix (recommended default):
- Authorization decisions (high level): 3 years for enterprise customers requiring long-term retention, 1 year default for hosted tenants.
- Identity snapshots: 1 year (or per customer contract).
- Provisioning events: 7 years for regulated customers (finance/health), 2 years default.
- SIEM-transient telemetry: 90 days hot, 1 year cold.
Notes: Retention is configurable by customer tier and contractual obligations; the actual retention policy id must be attached to the packaging manifest.

Secure SDLC checkpoints for auth and audit changes:
1. Design review: Security and IAM must review policy changes. Verify that audit events meet schema.
2. Tests: Unit tests to validate that events include required fields; integration tests to verify region_tag and pseudonymization.
3. Canary rollout: Apply policy change to a small percentage of traffic; monitor missing audit events and policy mismatches.
4. Evidence capture: During the canary, automatically store a time-windowed, read-only evidence bundle (retention per test policy).
5. Post-deployment audit: Compare expected vs. observed decisions and event rates; publish results to the change request.

Incident response — evidence preservation steps for authorization incidents (urgent):
1. Triage and declare impact window (UTC start/end).
2. Immediately toggle export to immutable storage for the impacted services (SRE action).
3. Snapshot IDP and role mappings (IAM export).
4. Freeze log rotation for the impacted window (prevent overwrite or purge).
5. Export canonical events and packaging manifest to secured evidence bucket (WORM if available).
6. Notify Compliance and Legal with evidence manifest and request a preservation hold.
7. If logs cross borders, consult with Legal before transferring; use pseudonymized copies if feasible.

Exception and risk-handling flow (authorization and residency exceptions):
1. Submit an exception request in the central Exceptions tracker with: owner, reason, scope, proposed compensating controls, duration, and rollback plan.
2. Risk review by Security + Legal within 5 business days.
3. If temporary approval granted, apply compensating controls (audit frequency increase, additional encryption at rest/in flight, restricted access to evidence artifacts).
4. Evidence of compensating controls must be attached to the exception ticket and included in any audit package.
5. Exception renewal: maximum 90 days without elevated executive approval.

SLOs and monitoring for audit pipelines:
- Ingestion availability: 99.95% monthly for audit events (platform SRE).
- Event delivery latency: 95th percentile under 5 seconds for same-region events; cross-region delivery under 30 seconds (subject to network).
- Retention enforcement: 100% of artifacts must have a retention policy id and observable enforcement (daily audit).
- Missing-field alerts: Critical if any required field is absent in more than 0.1% of events in a rolling 1-hour window.

Operational runbook snippets (examples):
- Extracting evidence bundle (CLI):
  1) Identify timeframe: export_start="2028-01-15T00:00:00Z"; export_end="2028-01-15T06:00:00Z"
  2) Run: rh-audit export --start $export_start --end $export_end --scope service:authz --format ndjson --out /tmp/evidence-20280115.ndjson
  3) Generate checksums: sha256sum /tmp/evidence-20280115.ndjson > /tmp/evidence-20280115.sha256
  4) Create manifest: rh-audit manifest create --input /tmp/evidence-20280115.ndjson --owner "Compliance Team" --policy-id retention-R1

- Example Elasticsearch query (redact client_ip when exporting for cross-border):
  POST _search
  {
    "query": {
      "bool": {
        "filter": [
          {"range": {"@timestamp": {"gte": "2028-01-15T00:00:00Z", "lt": "2028-01-16T00:00:00Z"}}},
          {"term": {"service": "authz"}}
        ]
      }
    }
  }

Audit packaging timeline (recommended):
- 0–2 business days: Initial artifact export and manifest generation.
- 2–5 business days: Evidence validation, pseudonymization summary, and checksum verification.
- 5–10 business days: Final packaging and compliance owner sign-off.

Checklist for cross-border evidence transfer requests:
- Confirm data classification and customer contractual constraints.
- Obtain Legal sign-off and record the decision in the exception tracker.
- Apply pseudonymization where required and record method in manifest.
- Limit export to minimal fields required by auditor.
- Record transport method and endpoint; prefer cloud-provider-native transfer within authorized regions.

Definitions and abbreviations:
- Authz: Authorization.
- Authn: Authentication.
- IAM: Identity & Access Management.
- WORM: Write Once Read Many.
- PII: Personally identifiable information.

Appendices:
A. Example manifest template (fields to include):
- manifest_id
- created_by
- created_at
- scope
- artifacts: list of artifact_filenames and checksums
- retention_policy_id
- pseudonymization_note
- signoff

B. Example evidence mapping table (textual representation):
- event_id -> commit_hash (policy change) -> canary_instance_ids -> retention_policy_id

C. Frequently asked questions (short):
Q: If a customer requests deletion of their logs in hosted deployments, how do we comply?
A: Verify contract, remove identifiable records, and if a full deletion is required, follow the cross-system purge playbook that removes both primary and replicated stores and generates a deletion manifest. For hybrid-residency customers, coordinate with the regional storage owner to ensure compliance.

D. Related controls and pages:
- IAM provisioning guidelines (link internal)

E. Revision history:
- 2027-11-01: Draft created by Aisha Patel.
- 2027-12-12: Added packaging checklist and retention matrix after tabletop review.
- 2028-02-15: Updated SLOs and cross-border checklist after Legal review.

If you are executing an evidence export or exception flow for the first time, open a ticket with Security (security-ops@redwood.com) so an on-call security engineer can validate the packaging and signatures prior to transfer.
